extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in media history and journalistic hoaxes
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying how a 19th-century newspaper hoax was constructed, promoted, and received, and what features made it persuasive and influential. Useful for studying sensationalist journalism, media ethics, and historical context of the penny press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism to increase sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that Locke was the author, his intentions were probably, first, to create a sensational story which would increase sales of The Sun
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames sensational content (exotic discoveries, vivid images) as a deliberate tactic to attract readers and advertisers; in the penny press business model, such stories helped papers thrive by drawing large numbers of readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of authoritative attribution to lend credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The discoveries were falsely attributed to Sir John Herschel and his fictitious companion Andrew Grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributing claims to a well-respected authority (real or plausibly real) increases perceived credibility and makes a fabricated story more persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated technical detail and vivid imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: These articles described animals..., trees, oceans and beaches. ... The telescope... lens measured '24 feet in diameter and 7 tons in weight'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing specific, concrete technical or sensory details and striking imagery (e.g., invented species, a gigantic telescope) increases plausibility and reader engagement; such detail is an effective device in hoaxes and satire but is an anti-pattern for honest reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical or ridicule intent versus deceptive intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Locke had meant for the hoax to act as a satire to show how science can be and is influenced by the thoughts of religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hoax may be designed as satire to ridicule ideas (here, extravagant astronomical theories); distinguishing stated satirical intent from outright deception is important when evaluating ethical implications and public harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication advertising/anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: The story was advertised on August 21, 1835, as an upcoming feature allegedly reprinted from The Edinburgh Courant. The first in a series of six was published four days later on August 25.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promoting a sensational feature in advance builds anticipation and increases initial circulation; coordinated advertising amplifies impact but can also amplify harm if the content is false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delayed correction or lack of retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: These articles were never retracted; however, on September 16, 1835, The Sun admitted the articles were in fact fabricated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to promptly correct or transparently retract false reporting affects public trust and can prolong misinformation; the timing and manner of admission are part of evaluating journalistic responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploitation of contemporary speculative science and public beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: The success of such sensational stories... can be partly attributed to the influence of contemporary speculative science. Figures like the Reverend Thomas Dick... had captured the public's imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoaxes that tap into prevailing beliefs, pseudoscientific claims, or authoritative-sounding scientific discourse are more likely to be believed; assessers should consider the cultural context that makes a claim plausible to its audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fabricated source/reprint claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The story was advertised... allegedly reprinted from The Edinburgh Courant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming a story is reprinted from another (supposedly reputable) source is a tactic to create the appearance of verification; fact-checking provenance is crucial in evaluating such pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invented narrators/personas as rhetorical device
rubrics_metrics.description: The author of the narrative was ostensibly Dr. Andrew Grant, the travelling companion and amanuensis of Sir John Herschel, but Grant was fictitious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating a plausible first-person narrator or witness can increase immersion and perceived authenticity; in evaluating work, verify the existence and credentials of named sources or narrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of plagiarism and literary controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Edgar Allan Poe claimed the story was a plagiarism of his earlier work 'The Unparalleled Adventure of One Hans Pfaall'... He later published 'The Balloon-Hoax' in the same newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoaxes and sensational pieces that closely resemble prior literary works risk accusations of plagiarism or unethical borrowing; such controversies affect authorial credibility and legacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penny press business model and topical choices
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sun was a pioneer... being the first New York newspaper to report on murders, suicides, personal events, and divorces, and it was because of stories such as these that the Sun thrived in attracting readers to their articles, and thus to their advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the economic incentives (advertising-driven circulation) that shape editorial choices; sensational topics were selected because they attracted readership and ad revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term impact on journalistic ethics and public perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The hoax reflected a time when readers were looking for entertainment as much as information from penny press newspapers, which would later change with the development of ethical reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating historical hoaxes, consider their role in the evolution of press ethics and how public expectations of news vs. entertainment have shifted over time.
